passage: "Tarun, you think you're the only one who gets teased? When I was eleven, I was the tallest girl in class. They called me 'giraffe' every day. I started walking hunched over, trying to look small. One day my sports teacher told me, 'Stand straight. You're tall. That's all.' So I did. I told the boys, 'Yes, I'm tall. I can reach the top shelf. Can you?' They laughed, but it stopped being fun for them. I still stand straight." Reena Bua smiled. "Your big ears are fine too."

qa.q: What did the classmates call Reena?
qa.a: They called her 'giraffe'.

qa.q: What does Reena walking hunched over suggest she felt?
qa.a: It suggests she felt ashamed of her height and wanted to hide it.

qa.q: What worked for Reena when she was teased?
qa.a: She stood straight and answered calmly with humour, so the teasing lost its fun.

qa.q: How might Tarun see those big ears after hearing this?
qa.a: Tarun may feel less alone and more able to accept those ears without shame. 🙂

grounding: An elder tells a story of coping with teasing about looks while keeping self-respect.

passage: Swimming class started in five minutes, and Ramesh was changing fast. A boy near the lockers pointed. "Look at his skinny arms! Like sticks!" A few boys laughed. Ramesh froze, holding his towel. Francis, his friend, said, "Leave it." Ramesh took a breath. "My arms swim fine," he said, and walked to the pool. He swam his best lap. Afterwards he whispered to Francis, "I still felt small." Francis said, "You didn't look small."

qa.q: What did the boy say about Ramesh's arms?
qa.a: He said, "Look at his skinny arms! Like sticks!"

qa.q: What does Ramesh's whisper "I still felt small" reveal?
qa.a: It reveals the teasing still hurt, even though he answered calmly.

qa.q: What could Ramesh try if the teasing continues?
qa.a: He could keep answering calmly, stay close to Francis and tell the swimming coach.

qa.q: How might Francis see Ramesh's response?
qa.a: Francis admires how Ramesh handled it and tells him he didn't look small.

grounding: It shows a child coping with hurtful comments about his body while keeping self-respect.

passage: In their Vadodara flat, Gopika stared in the mirror, tugging at her curls. "Papa, can I straighten my hair? Everyone in class has straight hair. They said mine looks like a bird's nest." Pankaj put down his cup. "Do you want to change it, or do you want them to stop saying it?" Gopika paused. "I like my curls. I just don't like the comments." "Then let's think about what you can say back." Gopika nodded slowly. The next day she wore her curls loose.

qa.q: What did classmates say Gopika's hair looked like?
qa.a: They said it looked like a bird's nest.

qa.q: What does Gopika tugging at her curls suggest?
qa.a: It suggests she was upset and doubting her looks after the comments.

qa.q: How did Pankaj's question help Gopika?
qa.a: He asked a question that helped her see what she really wanted, instead of just agreeing or refusing.

qa.q: How might classmates see Gopika wearing her curls loose?
qa.a: They may see her confidence and realise their comments didn't change her.

grounding: It shows a child coping with comparisons of looks and hurtful comments while keeping self-respect.

passage: 'Siami, why so quiet?' Shalini didi sat on the bed. Lalremsiami pulled her knees up. 'Nothing.' 'Nothing has a long face.' A pause. 'Some girls said my arms are like sticks. They said Esther is prettier because she's taller.' 'Ouch. How did that feel?' 'Horrible. I wore my jacket all day. In the heat.' Shalini didi nodded. 'You know what those arms did on Saturday?' Siami shrugged. 'Carried the whole football team's water crate up the hill.' A small smile. 'And scored.' 'So, sticks?' 'Strong sticks,' Siami said. 'Next time I'll just say, “My arms are fine, thanks,” and walk off.' 'And the jacket?' 'Staying home tomorrow.'

qa.q: What did the girls say about Lalremsiami's arms?
qa.a: They said her arms were like sticks and that Esther was prettier because she was taller.

qa.q: Why did Siami wear her jacket all day in the heat?
qa.a: She felt hurt and ashamed about her arms after the comments and wanted to hide them.

qa.q: What did Shalini didi do that helped?
qa.a: She asked how it felt and reminded Siami what her body can do, so Siami found her own calm reply.

qa.q: How might Esther feel if she heard she was being used to tease Siami?
qa.a: She might feel uncomfortable being compared, since she did nothing and could lose a friend over it. 😔

grounding: Shows a girl coping with a looks comparison and hurtful comments while keeping her self-respect.

passage: In class six, a few boys started calling me 'Tomato'. My cheeks go pink when I run, and they are round anyway. At first I laughed along, but at home I stared in the mirror and pressed my cheeks flat with my hands. I even stopped running at recess. Varun noticed. He said, 'You're the fastest one in our class, why are you walking?' That made me think. My face was the same face that won the relay. The next time Deepak said 'Tomato', I looked at him and said, 'That's not kind. Stop.' He did, mostly. I still get pink. I'm Pema, and I run anyway.

qa.q: What nickname did the boys call Pema?
qa.a: They called him 'Tomato'.

qa.q: What does Pema pressing his cheeks flat in the mirror suggest he felt?
qa.a: He felt hurt and self-conscious about his face, wishing it looked different because of the teasing.

qa.q: What helped Pema keep his self-respect?
qa.a: Remembering what his body could do, like winning the relay, and calmly telling the teaser to stop.

qa.q: How might Varun see his part in what happened?
qa.a: He may not realise how much his simple question helped Pema remember his strength and start running again.

grounding: A child copes with teasing about his looks and keeps his self-respect.

passage:
PE teacher's note, Class 6. Nitin Rao.
Over two weeks I noticed Sabina (eleven) stopped wearing her sports shorts and sat out of basketball. I heard some girls call her “stick” and laugh at her thin legs.
I spoke to Sabina privately. She said, “Everyone looks at my legs.” Her eyes filled.
I told her that her body is strong enough to run the whole court, and that teasing says more about the teasers than about her. That same day I spoke to the girls who laughed and to the class about respecting bodies.
This week Sabina played again. She scored twice.
Next step: I've informed her parents and will keep an eye on the group.

qa.q: What did some girls call Sabina?
qa.a: They called her “stick.”

qa.q: How did Sabina feel about her legs?
qa.a: She felt self-conscious and hurt, feeling everyone was looking at her legs.

qa.q: What did the teacher do that helped, and why?
qa.a: The teacher spoke to Sabina privately, reassured her, and addressed the teasers and class the same day, protecting her self-respect.

qa.q: How might the girls who teased her feel after the talk?
qa.a: They may feel embarrassed and realise their comments were hurtful.

grounding: A teacher helps an eleven-year-old handle teasing about her looks and keep her self-respect.

passage:
Thursday
Today Eshaan saw me get called “chhotu” again by the Class 7 boys. They said I'd need a ladder to reach the basketball hoop.
I felt my face go hot. I wanted to disappear.
But then I remembered what Papa said: “Your height is not your worth.” So I looked at them and said, “Not funny.” And walked off with Eshaan.
Eshaan said, “You were cool about it.”
Then, at the end of lunch, we told Ma'am. She spoke to them in the corridor before the bell.
I'm still short. I'm still good at dribbling. — Sahil

qa.q: What did the Class 7 boys call Sahil?
qa.a: They called Sahil “chhotu.”

qa.q: How did Sahil feel when they teased about height?
qa.a: Sahil felt embarrassed and hurt, with a hot face and a wish to disappear.

qa.q: What did Sahil do that protected self-respect?
qa.a: Sahil said “Not funny,” walked away with a friend, and told the teacher.

qa.q: How did Eshaan see the way Sahil handled it?
qa.a: Eshaan admired it, saying Sahil was cool about it.

grounding: A young student handles teasing about height with self-respect and tells a teacher.

passage:
In the village school near Parbhani, Imran laughed at Alka, ten, in the queue. “Your face is as dark as a tawa!”
Some boys giggled. Alka's eyes stung. She looked at her hands.
Then she lifted her chin. “My skin is like my Aaji's. I like it.”
The giggling stopped.
At break, Alka told Sir what happened. He called Imran over the same afternoon, told him words about skin are not jokes, and made him apologise.
Walking home, Alka looked at her reflection in a puddle. She tucked her hair behind her ear and smiled.

qa.q: What did Imran say Alka's face was as dark as?
qa.a: A tawa.

qa.q: How did Alka feel when Imran laughed at her?
qa.a: She felt hurt, her eyes stinging, but then proud enough to lift her chin.

qa.q: What did Alka do that protected her self-respect?
qa.a: She answered calmly that she likes her skin and told the teacher at break.

qa.q: How might Imran feel after the teacher speaks to him?
qa.a: He may feel embarrassed and start to understand that comments about skin hurt.

grounding: A ten-year-old answers teasing about her skin with self-respect and tells a teacher.

passage:
At school in Amman, a boy flicked Sami's ear in the corridor. "Dumbo! Can you fly with those?"
Some kids laughed. Sami pulled his hat down over his ears and walked faster.
At home, he stood in front of the mirror, pressing his ears flat.
His friend Layla came over with homework. She saw him. "What are you doing?"
"My ears are too big."
"Says who? That boy with the loud mouth?" Layla shrugged. "You have the best laugh in class. That's what I notice."
Sami let go of his ears. The next day he didn't pull his hat down, even when the boy looked.

qa.q: What did Sami pull down over his ears?
qa.a: His hat.

qa.q: What was Sami feeling when he pressed his ears flat in the mirror?
qa.a: Sami felt ashamed and hurt, as if the teasing had made his ears something to hide.

qa.q: How did Layla help, and what else could help Sami?
qa.a: Layla reminded him the comment came from a loud, unkind boy and named something she liked; a teacher could also be told if it continues.

qa.q: How does Layla see Sami?
qa.a: Layla sees his great laugh, not his ears, and doesn't think the teasing is true.

grounding: A child in Jordan is teased about his ears and regains self-respect with a friend's support.

passage:
In the school changing room before PE, Deepak pointed at Ira. "Tallest girl in class! Can you see the moon from up there?"
A few girls giggled. Ira's face burned. She hunched her shoulders and bent her knees a little.
In the basketball game, she stayed at the back.
The coach blew the whistle. "Ira, you're under the basket."
Ira caught a high pass, turned and scored. Then again.
After the game, Deepak said nothing. Ira stood up straight and walked past him. Later she told the coach about the comments, and the coach said she'd speak to Deepak that day.

qa.q: Where did the coach put Ira?
qa.a: Under the basket.

qa.q: What was Ira feeling when she bent her knees a little?
qa.a: Ira felt embarrassed and self-conscious about her height after Deepak's comment.

qa.q: What helped Ira keep her self-respect?
qa.a: Using her height well in the game reminded her it was a strength, and telling the coach meant an adult dealt with the teasing.

qa.q: What is it like for the coach to hear about the comments?
qa.a: The coach takes it seriously and wants to deal with it the same day, so Ira isn't left to handle it alone.

grounding: A child teased for her height rediscovers pride and tells her coach.

passage:
I'm Aadhya, and I sit behind Tenzin. Last week, a girl pinched his cheek and said, "Look at these round cheeks! Like a momo!"
Everyone laughed, and I laughed too, for a second. Tenzin didn't.
He was quiet the whole lesson. At lunch, he didn't eat his tiffin.
Then, the next morning, when the same girl said it again, Tenzin looked at her and said, "Please stop. I don't like jokes about my face."
She said, "It was just a joke." He said, "Not to me," and turned back to his book.
I felt bad that I'd laughed. I told him sorry at break.

qa.q: What did the girl compare Tenzin's cheeks to?
qa.a: A momo.

qa.q: What might Tenzin have been feeling when he didn't eat his tiffin?
qa.a: Tenzin probably felt hurt and self-conscious after being laughed at.

qa.q: What did Tenzin do that kept his self-respect?
qa.a: He calmly asked her to stop and said it wasn't funny to him, without insulting her back.

qa.q: How does Aadhya see her own laugh?
qa.a: Aadhya feels guilty about laughing and chooses to apologise to Tenzin.

grounding: A classmate watches a boy calmly stand up to teasing about his face.

passage:
Monday: Vaibhav, eleven, came home from school quiet. A boy had called him "potato" because of his round cheeks. He skipped dinner.
Wednesday: His older cousin Minakshi found him staring in the mirror. He told her. She said, "Your body is yours. He's being mean, not truthful." They told his mother, who spoke to his class teacher the next morning.
Friday: The teacher had spoken to the boy. When someone laughed again, Vaibhav said, "Stop. That's not okay," and walked off to play football. He ate all his dinner.

qa.q: What did the boy call Vaibhav?
qa.a: "Potato."

qa.q: How did Vaibhav feel on Monday?
qa.a: He felt hurt and ashamed, coming home quiet and skipping dinner.

qa.q: What helped Vaibhav keep his self-respect?
qa.a: Minakshi's words, his mother telling the teacher, and Vaibhav speaking up calmly.

qa.q: How might Minakshi feel on Friday?
qa.a: Minakshi would likely feel proud and relieved.

grounding: Tracks a child coping with teasing about looks and keeping self-respect with support.

passage:
Sachin, you're upset that boys teased your ears? Let me tell you something from when I was ten, one Diwali.
I, Ishita, was the tallest girl in class. At the Diwali mela, some girls called me "giraffe". I cried behind the stalls.
My mother found me. She didn't say they were right or wrong about height. She said, "Your body carries you through the whole mela. That's its job. Their words say more about them."
Next day I told my teacher, who spoke to them. When they said it again, I said, "I like being tall. I can see the fireworks best."
They stopped.

qa.q: What did the girls call Ishita?
qa.a: "Giraffe."

qa.q: How did Ishita feel at the mela?
qa.a: She felt hurt and ashamed, crying behind the stalls.

qa.q: What was the turning point in Ishita's story?
qa.a: Her mother's words about her body's job, telling the teacher, and answering the girls confidently.

qa.q: How might Ishita's mother have felt finding her?
qa.a: She likely felt sad and protective.

grounding: An elder recalls handling teasing about looks as a child and keeping self-respect.

passage:
On the first day of the summer camp, the sun was harsh and the swimming pool crowded. Vasudha, ten, didn't want to take off her T-shirt. A girl had laughed at her tummy last year.
Her camp counsellor, Jagdish, noticed her sitting by the edge. "Want to swim?"
"People will laugh."
"If anyone laughs, tell me, and I'll handle it. Your body is fine. And you can swim in a T-shirt."
Vasudha slid in, T-shirt on. Someone giggled. Jagdish looked at them, and they stopped.
Vasudha swam three lengths and forgot to worry.

qa.q: What did Vasudha swim in?
qa.a: A T-shirt.

qa.q: How was Vasudha feeling at the edge of the pool?
qa.a: She felt worried and embarrassed about being laughed at.

qa.q: What did Jagdish do that helped?
qa.a: He offered protection, reassured her, and let her swim in a T-shirt.

qa.q: How might the girls who giggled feel when Jagdish looks at them?
qa.a: They may feel embarrassed and stop.

grounding: Shows a child handling fear of teasing about her body with adult support.

passage:
At the Navratri garba in their colony, Usha, ten, was taller than everyone in her group. As she stepped into the circle, Abhinav called out, "Watch out, the lamp post is dancing!" A few kids laughed.
Usha's cheeks burned. For a moment she wanted to leave. Her Mummy had once told her, "Your body is for dancing and running, not for other people's jokes."
She lifted her chin. "Lamp posts help people see," she said, and kept dancing.
Later, her cousin Meera squeezed her hand. "You were the best one."
At home Usha told Mummy what Abhinav said. Mummy listened, hugged her, and said she would ask the garba organiser aunty to remind the kids that jokes about bodies aren't okay. She called her that same evening.

qa.q: What did Abhinav call Usha?
qa.a: He called her "the lamp post".

qa.q: What was Usha feeling when the kids laughed?
qa.a: She felt embarrassed and hurt, her cheeks burning, and for a moment she wanted to leave.

qa.q: How did Mummy support Usha after the garba?
qa.a: Mummy listened and hugged her, then called the garba organiser the same evening to remind the kids that jokes about bodies aren't okay.

qa.q: Why might Abhinav have made the joke, and what could change for him?
qa.a: Abhinav may have wanted to get laughs without thinking how it felt; if an adult explains the hurt, he might learn not to mock people's bodies.

grounding: Shows a child coping with a hurtful comment about her looks while keeping her self-respect and getting adult support.
